newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: FEATURE-Colombian rebel sets sights on march into capital.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Colombian rebel sets sights on march into capital.

text.p: The wiry rebel commander perches on a log in his sprawling jungle base camp and shrugs at suggestions he is one of the biggest thorns in the side of the military.

As head of the Southern Bloc of the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia (FARC), Joaquin Gomez has dealt the army two of its most crushing defeats in more than three decades of political bloodletting. But the man known in rebel ranks as Comrade Joaquin or simply "Joaco" spoke modestly of himself, if not his goals, in a rare interview with Reuters this month.

"I'm just another guerrilla fighter in the lines. My greatest aspiration is to defend the interests of the great majorities," he said. "These actions are the work of everybody," he said of his two major victories in the past year. "I'm not a loose wheel."

Gomez took over as head of the bloc in the early 1990s but shot to notoriety in April 1996 when he ordered a fiery ambush that left 31 soldiers dead in southern Narino province. Then in August he orchestrated a raid on the Las Delicias army base in southern Putumayo province in which another 31 soldiers died and 60 were captured.

The prisoners were released more than nine months later, on June 15, after the FARC -- Latin America's oldest and largest rebel force -- succeeded in wringing a huge political concession from the government, the temporary demilitarization of a huge swathe of Caqueta province.
Gomez gives credit for the attack and subsequent release to the FARC's supreme leader, Manuel "Sureshot" Marulanda, whom he calls a "great political and military visionary."

The 50-year-old Gomez, originally from deeply impoverished Guajira province in the north, joined the FARC 12 years ago on his return from a long period of studies in the Soviet Union. In Moscow he acquired the complete works of Karl Marx in Russian -- his constant albeit weighty companion during long treks through the jungle and across the mountains of southern Colombia. It was there too that he first laid eyes on what was to become his weapon of choice -- the sturdy Russian-made AK-47 assault rifle, known as the "rebels' favourite."

Since its formation as a pro-Soviet guerrilla army in 1964, the FARC has mushroomed from 48 men to more than 18,000 mostly peasant fighters and has de facto control over about 50 percent of the country, according to independent political analysts. It is still fighting a hit-and-run guerrilla war and has not moved to set up liberated zones, which would inevitably draw it into a war of positions with the army. But Gomez rejected claims that it lacks any long-term objectives.

"I aspire one day to march into the Plaza Bolivar as the result of our victory," he said, referring to Bogota's main square, a stone's throw from the presidential palace. "The route (to that victory) is not foreseeable because both political and military means are valid. But how long our struggle lasts depends on our force of arms," he added.
REBELS LOOK TO CREATE NEW COLOMBIA

The relevance of the armed strugle, Gomez contended, has not faded with the fall of the Berlin Wall. "When we first picked up the gun there was hunger and social injustice. The wall has fallen but those injustices remain in Colombia. Our aim is to create a more just society where the abysmal differences between those that have and those that have not are less. We're looking for peace with social justice."

Despite those high aims, tactics of the FARC, including mass kidnappings, have come under severe questioning in light of persistent allegations by the government and military that the FARC has become the country's No. 1 drug mob.

Gomez denied those allegations but defended the right of peasants to grow coca, the raw material for cocaine, as the only means of survival in a region of "socio-economic abandonment." He also defended kidnapping, which he said was a "political act" that the FARC used to strengthen the "people's army" while the state built up its "war machine" on the back of general taxation.

"I just feel that unfortunately we've done what we had to do," he said. "We're not here because we hate life but because we love it. We're here because we want to conquer a new Colombia where we can all live and have a secure future."
